Paper_name: The automatic and the expected self: separating self- and familiarity biases effects by manipulating stimulus probability
Summary: The study investigated whether prepotent responses to self-associated stimuli can be modulated by their frequency of occurrence. Participants associated shapes with self, mother, or a stranger and performed a sequential shape-label matching task where the probability of different pairings was varied. A robust self-advantage was found across all conditions. Reducing the proportion of self-related trials did not weaken performance for self stimuli, whereas reducing the frequency of mother or stranger trials impaired performance. Self-related biases occurred automatically even when self stimuli had a low probability, and expectations for frequent self-stimuli operated exclusively, minimizing biases to other high-probability stimuli.
Author: Jie Sui, Yang Sun, Kaiping Peng, Glyn W. Humphreys
Conclusion: Biases favoring self-related stimuli occur automatically and are not weakened even when self-related stimuli occur infrequently. Expectations for high-probability self-stimuli operate in an exclusive manner, minimizing biases to other frequent stimuli. In contrast, biases to high-familiarity stimuli (e.g., mother) can be reduced when they occur infrequently and do not dominate expectations over other high-frequency stimuli.
